exampleAnswers.title: Applying the Pythagorean Theorem to the Unit Circle

question.text: The point $P$ is located in the third quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $-\dfrac{3}{5}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $P?$
question.explanation:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem:

\[ x^2+y^2=1 \]

Substituting $y=-\dfrac 3 5$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives \begin{align*} x^2+y^2&=1\\[5pt] x^2+ \left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^2&=1\\[5pt] x^2+\left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right)&=1\\[5pt] x^2&= 1-\dfrac{9}{25}\\[5pt] x^2& = \dfrac{16}{25}\\[5pt] x &= \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{{16}}{25}}\\[5pt] x& = \pm \dfrac{4}{5}. \end{align*}

Finally, we select the negative answer since $x$ is negative in the third quadrant. So our final answer is $x = -\dfrac{4}{5}.$

question.text: The point $P$ is located in the second quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $\dfrac{5}{7}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $P?$
question.explanation:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem:

\[ x^2+y^2=1 \]

Substituting $y=\dfrac 5 7$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives \begin{align*} x^2+y^2&=1\\[5pt] x^2+ \left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)^2&=1\\[5pt] x^2+\left(\dfrac{25}{49}\right)&=1\\[5pt] x^2&= 1-\dfrac{25}{49}\\[5pt] x^2& = \dfrac{24}{49}\\[5pt] x &= \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{{24}}{49}}\\[5pt] x& = \pm \dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}. \end{align*}

Finally, we select the negative answer since $x$ is negative in the second quadrant. So our final answer is $x = -\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $ \sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4},$ what is the value of $\cos \theta?$
question.explanation:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \cos^2\theta &= 1 - \sin^2\theta\\[3pt] \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$ gives

\begin{align*} \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{7}{16}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{16}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{3}{4}. \end{align*}

We select the negative answer since $\cos\theta$ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac {3}{4}.$

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $ \cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2},$ what is the value of $\sin \theta?$
question.explanation:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \sin^2\theta &= 1 - \cos^2\theta\\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$ gives

\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. \end{align*}

We select the negative answer since $\sin\theta$ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = -\dfrac {\sqrt {3}}{2}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $ \sin\theta=\dfrac{4}{5},$ what is the value of $\cot\theta?$
question.explanation:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \cos^2\theta &= 1 - \sin^2\theta\\[3pt] \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}$ gives

\begin{align*} \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{16}{25}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{25}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{3}{5}. \end{align*}

We select the negative answer since $\cos\theta$ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac {3}{5}.$

Finally, knowing that $\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ we have \[ \cot \theta = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)} = -\dfrac{3}{4}. \]

example.title: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $ \cos\theta=\dfrac{8}{9},$ what is the value of $\tan\theta?$
question.explanation:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \sin^2\theta &= 1 - \cos^2\theta\\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{8}{9}$ gives

\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{64}{81}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{17}{81}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt {17}}{9}. \end{align*}

We select the negative answer since $\sin\theta$ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = -\dfrac {\sqrt {17}}{9}.$

Finally, knowing that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},$ we have \[ \tan \theta = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{9}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right)} =- \dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{8}. \]

example.title: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: If $\csc \theta = \dfrac{5}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi$ then what is the value of $\tan \theta+\cot\theta?$
question.explanation:
As $\csc\theta=\dfrac{5}{3}$ then $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\csc\theta}=\dfrac{3}{5}.$

Let's sketch our angle $\theta$ in the coordinate plane.

We're given that $\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \cos^2\theta &= 1 - \sin^2\theta\\[3pt] \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}$ gives

\begin{align*} \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{25}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{16}{25}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{4}{5}. \end{align*}

We select the negative answer since $\cos\theta$ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{4}{5}.$

Finally, knowing that $\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ and $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ we have:

  • $\cot\theta= \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$

  • $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)} =-\dfrac{3}{4}.$

Finally, we have

$\tan\theta + \cot\theta = -\dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{3}{4} = -\dfrac{25}{12}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: If $\cos \theta = -\dfrac{9}{10}$ and $90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$ then what is the value of $\csc \theta?$
question.explanation:
Let's sketch our angle $\theta$ in the coordinate plane.

We're given that $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{9}{10}.$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \sin^2\theta &= 1 - \cos^2\theta\\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{9}{10}$ gives

\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(-\dfrac{9}{10}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{81}{100}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{19}{100}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{19}}{10}. \end{align*}

We select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the second quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt {19}}{10}.$

Finally, knowing that $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have \[ \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt {19}}{10}\right)} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt {19}} = \dfrac{10\sqrt {19}}{19}. \]

example.title: Computing a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $ \dfrac{1}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\csc\theta.$
question.explanation:
We're given that $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \sin^2\theta &= 1 - \cos^2\theta\\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}$ gives

\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{16}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{15}{16}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{4}. \end{align*}

Finally, we select the negative answer since $\sin\theta$ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So $\sin\theta = -\dfrac {\sqrt {15}}{4}.$

Finally, knowing that $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have \[ \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(-\dfrac {\sqrt {15}}{4}\right)} = -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{15}} =- \dfrac {4\sqrt {15}}{15}. \]
